The CBO's focus on SNAP’s link to food choices and healthcare costs is spot-on. For years, SNAP’s lax nutrition standards have funneled taxpayer dollars into sugary drinks and ultra-processed junk, fueling diabetes and heart disease. Studies show SNAP participants have higher rates of diet-related illnesses than income-eligible nonparticipants, costing billions in avoidable Medicaid and Medicare spending.

The real issue isn’t just "food deserts"—it’s policy deserts. Programs like GusNIP prove incentivizing fruits and vegetables works, yet the 2023 Farm Bill still lets SNAP subsidize the same processed garbage that hospitalizes low-income Americans.

If Congress wants fiscal sanity, they’ll slash SNAP’s $140B budget for Big Food handouts and redirect funds to real food. Otherwise, taxpayers keep bankrolling the chronic disease crisis.

Modernizing Social Security's paper-based processes is long overdue, but half of medical records still arriving via fax in 2025 shows bureaucratic inertia. While Commissioner Bisignano's focus on digitization aligns with the $30M TMF investment for document upload platforms, the continued reliance on 20th-century tech like fax machines proves D.C.'s modernization theater.
